connector: You’ve seen Germany take over Denmark, and you’ve seen the Danish king riding through the streets of Copenhagen. Today’s reading is about a law the Nazis made in many countries, a law that marked Jewish people with a yellow star. Denmark’s answer was different. Pay close attention to why.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. Today’s reading is about a law the Nazis made in many countries, forcing Jewish people to wear a yellow star. It’s a hard subject, and an important one. You’ll also learn how Denmark’s answer was different. Then you’ll study one sentence that says a hard truth very carefully, and try writing one like it.
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is holding on to a puzzle. Sometimes a fact doesn’t make sense yet, and that’s fine. Mark it, make a guess, and keep reading. The new book is called Number the Stars. Keep that title in your mind today, and see whether anything you read helps it make sense.
transcripts.dol: Pick the sentence you’d like to fix. Both have the same troubles: lost capitals, and two sentences pressed together. Look closely at the model on top. Some words there are names of peoples and groups, and those always take a capital, wherever they fall in the sentence.
transcripts.guide1: Today the word work asks you to build, not just find. You’ll choose the right word and write it in yourself. When you’re unsure, say the sentence out loud with each choice. Your ear often catches what your eye misses. Then check, and fix anything that didn’t sound right.
transcripts.morphology: Two spans of the bridge are finished, and the lamps at their ends are lit. Today you build the third. The same two word parts are doing the work, one meaning across and one meaning forward. Read every meaning all the way through before you choose. The meaning is your map.
transcripts.vocabulary: Today’s words come from the reading about the yellow star. Some of them are hard words for a hard subject, and they matter. Read the sentence above each one carefully. Think about what the word is doing in that sentence before you guess. Then flip the card, and see how close you came.
transcripts.grammar: This time you supply the word yourself. Read each sentence and ask one question: is the missing person doing the action, or is the action happening to them? That decides which form you need. Use the word bank, and say each finished sentence out loud to check it.
transcripts.spelling: Today you fill in the missing vowel pair yourself. There are two decisions for each word: which pair belongs, and how it sounds in that spot. If you’re stuck, say the whole word slowly and stretch out the middle. The sound usually points to the pair.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about ordinary people: teachers, fishermen, doctors, neighbors. Most of their courage was small and quiet. A doctor who wrote a different name on a hospital record. A neighbor who kept a child safe for a week. One small act doesn’t look like much. Thousands of them, together, saved thousands of lives.
transcripts.read: This passage begins with what happened in many countries, and then it turns. Watch for the word different. That’s where Denmark’s part begins. There’s also a famous story in here that isn’t quite true. As you read, think about why people might keep telling it anyway.
transcripts.rwm: Look at where today’s sentence pauses. The writer could have stopped early. Instead, a dash holds you still for a moment, and then two more words tell the harder truth. A pause like that makes the end land with weight. Writers save it for the words that matter most.
transcripts.guide3: Time to write. Today’s questions ask you to explain a law, compare Denmark to other countries, and think about a story that isn’t exactly true. Take your time with that last one. You’ll also try the writer’s sentence shape from the reading, and take today’s step in your own writing.
transcripts.chapter: The last question is the most interesting one today. A story can be untrue and still tell you something true about the people who told it. Ask yourself what the Danes wanted to believe about their king, and about themselves. Then use the passage to show how you know.
transcripts.workshop: A claim has to be something a person could argue with. If no one could ever disagree, it’s just a fact. Today you’ll test your claims. Could a smart, fair person say no? If not, change it until they could. That’s when a claim is ready for reasons.

a.raw: the danish king stood with his jewish people he refused the nazi rule
a.fixed: The Danish king stood with his Jewish people. He refused the Nazi rule.
a.why: Capitals on The, Danish, Jewish and Nazi, a period after people, a capital H to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: the danish government refused the star law the nazis did not force it
b.fixed: The Danish government refused the star law. The Nazis did not force it.
b.why: Capitals on The, Danish and Nazis, a period after law to end the first sentence, a capital T to start the second, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q2: … and say what Denmark’s choice tells you about its leaders.
scholar.journal-q3: … and connect it to King Christian’s rides from the last lesson’s Courage Watch.

g4w15ff1.h1: Someone is doing the hiding, and it’s more than one person. Which word in the bank does an action?
g4w15ff1.why: They does the action (hid), so it takes the subject form, with a capital to start the sentence.

g4w15ff2.h1: The soldier does the questioning. The missing word is the girl it happens to.
g4w15ff2.why: her receives the action (questioned), so it takes the object form.

g4w15ff3.h1: This person is doing the carrying, and it was her shoe.
g4w15ff3.why: She does the action (carried), so it takes the subject form, with a capital to start the sentence.

g4w15ff4.h1: Nobody is the one telling. The missing word is the boy who didn’t get told.
g4w15ff4.why: him receives the action (told), so it takes the object form.

s4w15ff1.h1: The middle of achieve says a long E. Two pairs in the bank can spell that sound; this one starts with i.

s4w15ff2.h1: Retreat ends like treat. Which pair spells the long E in eat and seat?

s4w15ff3.h1: The end of campaign sounds like rain. Which pair spells the long A in rain?
s4w15ff3.why: ai: campaign. The g is silent, the way it is in sign.

s4w15ff4.h1: Neutral starts with a sound like new. Which pair is left in the bank?

match.occupation: Occupation is about one country taking control of another. Look for the meaning about taking over.
match.resistance: Resistance means pushing back. Look for the meaning about standing up against something wrong.
match.deport: Deport is about being sent out of a country. Look for the meaning about being forced to leave.
match.rescue: To rescue someone is to get them out of danger. Look for the meaning about saving.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Each right word lays a plank and the bridge reaches forward.

why.t: This week is a bridge between two books, from Anne’s island to Denmark, where Number the Stars takes place. trans- means across, so each word lays a plank across the water. pro- means forward, so the bridge reaches forward, one span each lesson, until it touches the far shore.

wordgame.win: The bridge reaches the far shore, and every lamp is lit. trans- = across, pro- = forward. Next week, the story begins.

notes.wgrd: Some facts don’t make sense yet. Mark the puzzling fact, guess why the author of the novel wants you to know it, and check your guess when the story begins.
vocab: To make something a rule that people must follow.
A person or thing that someone is aiming to hurt or attack.
To say no; to decide not to do something.
Something worn on clothing to show who a person is or what group they belong to.
When one country takes over and controls another.
Standing up against something you believe is wrong.
To force someone to leave a country, usually against their will.
notes.wordParts: trans- means “across” (transatlantic, transport). pro- means “forward” (propose, progress).
notes.grammar: Use the subject form when the person does the action (They waited) and the object form when the action happens to them (The guard stopped them).
notes.spelling: Two decisions for each vowel team: which pair spells the sound you hear, and whether that part of the word is stressed. A long E can be spelled ie or ea; a long A can be spelled ai or ay.
